landing.html.find: For Jewish friends — the case from the Tanakh, the Targum and the Talmud, and the history to name first.
landing.html.replace: For Jewish friends — the case made from books they already hold: the Hebrew Bible, the old Aramaic translation of it, and the Talmud. Plus the history to name before anything else.
landing.html.why: three unexplained Hebrew and Aramaic proper nouns in a single card on the front door — the exact moment a non-theology reader decides the site is not for them

landing.html.find: <meta name="description" content="Faith claims, examined against the Bible — with honest verdicts, cited sources, and scripted conversations.">
landing.html.replace: <meta name="description" content="What other faiths teach, weighed against the Bible — with straight verdicts, sources you can check, and the words to say in a real conversation.">
landing.html.why: "Faith claims" and "scripted conversations" are how the builder describes the site, not how a visitor would. NOTE: the identical sentence also sits in the og:description on line 8 — change both, but only this one can be matched uniquely.

about-src.html.find: Steelman first. Every claim carries the strongest published defense from that faith's own scholars, before any verdict is given.
about-src.html.replace: Give the other side its best shot first. Every claim here is shown with the strongest published defence from that faith's own scholars before any verdict is given — a habit usually called steelmanning, the opposite of knocking down a straw man.
about-src.html.why: "Steelman first" is the very first rule on the About page and the first thing many readers see, and it is a term from online-argument culture. Keeping the word but leading with the plain version teaches it instead of gatekeeping with it.

about-src.html.find: IslamQA and the classical tafsir for Islam.
about-src.html.replace: IslamQA and the classical tafsir — the traditional Muslim verse-by-verse commentaries on the Quran — for Islam.
about-src.html.why: "tafsir" appears in a list of otherwise recognisable names, so the reader cannot tell whether they have missed something

about-src.html.find: Verdicts are editorial. They describe the state of the public argument as best we can determine it — they are judgments, not revelations, and they cite their reasons.
about-src.html.replace: The verdicts are our judgement, not God's. Each one describes where the public argument currently stands, as best we can tell, and shows the reasons behind it. They are calls we have made, and you can check our working.
about-src.html.why: "editorial" is publishing-trade vocabulary and "the state of the public argument" is abstract, on a point the reader most needs to trust

about-src.html.find: and makes the case for the Bible where it is not yet shared ground
about-src.html.replace: and makes the case for the Bible itself where the reader does not already accept it
about-src.html.why: "shared ground" is debate vocabulary in the site's opening sentence

about-src.html.find: Around forty entries across the site exist purely to tell Christians to stop using an argument
about-src.html.replace: Around forty entries on this site exist for one purpose: to tell Christians to stop using a particular argument
about-src.html.why: "entries" plus "exist purely to" reads as catalogue-speak in the middle of the page's best and most human idea

parallels-src.html.find: It's a tu quoque — an argument from mutual embarrassment — and it proves nothing about whether either claim is true.
parallels-src.html.replace: It is the "well, you too" move — arguing by mutual embarrassment — and it proves nothing about whether either claim is actually true.
parallels-src.html.why: leading with untranslated Latin makes the reader feel excluded exactly where the page is trying to teach humility. The plain name comes first; the point is unchanged.

parallels-src.html.find: Tahrif — but corruption of the text is a
parallels-src.html.replace: Tahrif, the charge that the Bible was corrupted — but corruption of the text itself is a
parallels-src.html.why: "Tahrif" is styled as a keyword and then never defined on this page, in a table cell the reader is meant to scan in seconds

parallels-src.html.find: The seal of the prophets, with
parallels-src.html.replace: Muhammad as the seal of the prophets — the last one, after whom no more come — with
parallels-src.html.why: "the seal of the prophets" is a title, not a description, and it is doing the whole work of that cell
"jurisprudence" and "prescribes" are two law-school words where two everyday words say the same thing

parallels-src.html.find: which is precisely why a luminous messenger is not self-authenticating
parallels-src.html.replace: which is precisely why a shining messenger cannot vouch for himself
parallels-src.html.why: "self-authenticating" is philosophy-of-religion vocabulary landing at the end of the page's key paragraph

parallels-src.html.find: <small>Placed beyond correction — either by being inspired, or by not being inspired and still being obeyed</small>
parallels-src.html.replace: <small>Put beyond correction — either by claiming to speak for God, or by admitting it does not and still requiring obedience</small>
parallels-src.html.why: the clever inversion works only for a reader who already knows what "inspired" means as a technical term; spelled out, it is sharper

parallels-src.html.find: A movement that claims a new revelation correcting the Bible tends to need the same set of parts to work — a private channel, a reason the existing Scriptures can't be trusted, and a cost for leaving.
parallels-src.html.replace: A movement that claims a new message from God correcting the Bible tends to need the same set of parts to work — someone who heard it privately, a reason the existing Scriptures can't be trusted, and a price for walking away.
parallels-src.html.why: "revelation" and "a private channel" are the two abstractions the whole page rests on, in the paragraph that first states the thesis
